sections.content: Rather than commit hundreds of engineers to every idea, Snap formed a small team of design engineers who could handle the product design and engineering process and build early versions. They put prototypes into the Snapchat app and tested them in places such as Australia or a few high schools, observing user behavior and gathering real-world data without first building the product to production level. Gaurav emphasized the value of getting a product into users’ hands, since an idea that looks good in design may prove unhelpful in use.

sections.content: The sequence was to build quickly, get the prototype out, collect feedback, and understand whether it worked. Once the team understood the product and its dynamics, it could bring in the engineering team to build at scale—an investment described as potentially 500 engineers for six months. This pretesting mattered because a failed idea after a 500-engineer, year-long effort would be costly.

answer.summary: Snap used a small design-engineering team to prototype ideas in the Snapchat app and test them with real users before investing in a production-scale build.

sections.heading: Prototype and test before scaling
sections.content: As Snap grew, a new product could require hundreds of engineers for months, making a failed bet costly. Gaurav described creating a small team of “design engineers” who could handle the product design and engineering process and put early versions directly into Snapchat. They tested prototypes in places such as Australia or a few high schools, observed how people behaved, and gathered real-world data without first building the product to production level. Once they understood whether it worked and its product dynamics, they could bring in the engineering team to scale it—rather than committing 500 engineers for six months or a year upfront.

sections.heading: Core principle
sections.content: The approach was to get something into users’ hands, learn from actual use, and use that feedback to decide whether to invest further; Gaurav emphasized that a design that looks good under ideal conditions may prove unhelpful when people actually try it.
